**David McDowell Brown** (April 16, 1956 – February 1, 2003) was a [United States Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Navy "United States Navy")[captain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain_(United_States_O-6) "Captain (United States O-6)") and [NASA astronaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_astronaut "NASA astronaut"). He died on his first [spaceflight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spaceflight "Spaceflight"), when the [Space Shuttle _Columbia_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia") ([STS-107](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-107 "STS-107")) disintegrated during orbital reentry into the Earth's atmosphere. Brown became an astronaut in 1996 but had not served on a space mission prior to the [_Columbia_ disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia disaster"). He was posthumously awarded the [Congressional Space Medal of Honor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congressional_Space_Medal_of_Honor "Congressional Space Medal of Honor").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_M._Brown#cite_note-1)

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=David_M._Brown&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Brown was born on April 16, 1956, in [Arlington, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arlington,_Virginia "Arlington, Virginia"). As a youth, he attended McKinley Elementary School and Swanson Middle School, and graduated from [Yorktown High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yorktown_High_School_(Virginia) "Yorktown High School (Virginia)") in Arlington in 1974. Brown was a member of the [Boy Scouts of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boy_Scouts_of_America "Boy Scouts of America") and achieved its second-highest rank, [Life Scout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_Scout "Life Scout"). [[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_M._Brown#cite_note-:0-2) He received a [Bachelor of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Science "Bachelor of Science") degree in [biology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biology "Biology") from the [College of William & Mary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_of_William_&_Mary "College of William & Mary") in 1978, and a [Doctor of Medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_of_Medicine "Doctor of Medicine") from the [Eastern Virginia Medical School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Virginia_Medical_School "Eastern Virginia Medical School") in 1982.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_M._Brown#cite_note-:0-2)

## Military career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=David_M._Brown&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Military career")]

Brown joined the [U.S. Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Navy "U.S. Navy") after his internship at the [Medical University of South Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_University_of_South_Carolina "Medical University of South Carolina"). Upon completion of [flight surgeon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flight_surgeon "Flight surgeon") training in 1984, Brown reported to the Navy Branch Hospital in [Adak, Alaska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adak,_Alaska "Adak, Alaska"), as Director of Medical Services.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_M._Brown#cite_note-3) He was then assigned to [Carrier Air Wing Fifteen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carrier_Air_Wing_Fifteen "Carrier Air Wing Fifteen") which deployed aboard the [aircraft carrier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aircraft_carrier "Aircraft carrier")[USS _Carl Vinson_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Carl_Vinson "USS Carl Vinson") in the Western Pacific. In 1988, Brown became the only flight surgeon in a 10-year period to be chosen for pilot training. He was ultimately designated a [Naval Aviator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naval_Aviator "Naval Aviator") in 1990 at [NAS Chase Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAS_Chase_Field "NAS Chase Field") in [Beeville, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beeville,_Texas "Beeville, Texas"), ranking number one in his class. Brown was then sent for training and carrier qualification in the [A-6E Intruder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A-6_Intruder "A-6 Intruder"). In 1991, he reported to the Naval Strike Warfare Center at [NAS Fallon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAS_Fallon "NAS Fallon"), [Nevada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nevada "Nevada"), serving as a Strike Leader Attack Training Syllabus Instructor and a Contingency Cell Planning Officer. Brown was also qualified in the [F/A-18 Hornet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F/A-18_Hornet "F/A-18 Hornet") and deployed from Japan in 1992 aboard [USS _Independence_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Independence_(CV-62) "USS Independence (CV-62)") flying the A-6E with [VA-115](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VFA-115 "VFA-115"). In 1995, he reported to the [U.S. Naval Test Pilot School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Naval_Test_Pilot_School "U.S. Naval Test Pilot School") at [NAS Patuxent River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAS_Patuxent_River "NAS Patuxent River"), Maryland as their flight surgeon, where Brown also flew the [T-38 Talon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T-38_Talon "T-38 Talon").

Brown logged over 2,700 flight hours, with 1,700 in high-performance military aircraft. He was qualified as the first pilot in NASA T-38 aircraft and held a [Federal Communications Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Communications_Commission "Federal Communications Commission") (FCC) issued Technician Class [amateur radio license](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amateur_radio_license "Amateur radio license") with the [call sign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Call_sign "Call sign") KC5ZTC.

Brown also served as President of the International Association of Military Flight Surgeon Pilots, an associate fellow at the [Aerospace Medical Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerospace_Medical_Association "Aerospace Medical Association"), and a member of the Society of U.S. Naval Flight Surgeons.

## NASA career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=David_M._Brown&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: NASA career")]

Selected by [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA") in April 1996, Brown reported to the [Johnson Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_Space_Center "Johnson Space Center") in August 1996. He completed two years of training and evaluation and was qualified for flight assignment as a mission specialist. Brown was initially assigned to support payload development for the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station"), followed by the astronaut support team responsible for orbiter cockpit setup, crew strap-in, and landing recovery.

On April 21, 2001, Brown appeared on [ESPN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESPN "ESPN") as an expert on [g-force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G-force "G-force") loading on the human body that led to the cancellation of the [Firestone Firehawk 600](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Firestone_Firehawk_600 "Firestone Firehawk 600")[CART](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Championship_Auto_Racing_Teams "Championship Auto Racing Teams") race.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_M._Brown#cite_note-4)

Brown flew aboard [Space Shuttle _Columbia_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia") on [STS-107](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-107 "STS-107"), logging 15 days, 22 hours, and 20 minutes in space from January 16 to February 1, 2003. The flight was a dedicated science and research mission. Working 24 hours a day, in two alternating shifts, the crew successfully conducted approximately 80 experiments. On February 1, 2003, all seven members of _Columbia'_ s crew perished during reentry, 16 minutes before the scheduled landing.

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=David_M._Brown&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Personal life")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fe/US_Navy_030312-N-2147L-001_U.S._Navy_Capt._David_M._Brown%2C_NASA_Astronaut_laid_to_rest.jpg/250px-US_Navy_030312-N-2147L-001_U.S._Navy_Capt._David_M._Brown%2C_NASA_Astronaut_laid_to_rest.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:US_Navy_030312-N-2147L-001_U.S._Navy_Capt._David_M._Brown,_NASA_Astronaut_laid_to_rest.jpg)

Brown's funeral services at [Arlington National Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arlington_National_Cemetery "Arlington National Cemetery") on March 12, 2003

The only unmarried member of the STS-107 crew, Brown had previously been romantically involved with NASA engineer Ann Micklos. The couple ended their relationship shortly before the mission and remained close friends until his death.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_M._Brown#cite_note-5) The crew of STS-107 had formed a close friendship during their training, and Brown had been preparing a video to commemorate this once they returned from the mission. He is buried in [Arlington National Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arlington_National_Cemetery "Arlington National Cemetery").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_M._Brown#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_M._Brown#cite_note-7)

## Tributes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=David_M._Brown&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Tributes")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0f/David_M._Brown_Planetarium%2C_Arlington%2C_Virginia_.jpg/250px-David_M._Brown_Planetarium%2C_Arlington%2C_Virginia_.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:David_M._Brown_Planetarium,_Arlington,_Virginia_.jpg)

The David M. Brown Planetarium in Arlington County, Virginia

*   Asteroid [51825 Davidbrown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/51825_Davidbrown "51825 Davidbrown") was named in honor of Brown.
*   Lunar crater D. Brown is named after Brown.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_M._Brown#cite_note-8)
*   Brown Hall, in the Columbia Village apartments, at the [Florida Institute of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida_Institute_of_Technology "Florida Institute of Technology") is named after him.
*   He is the first person to be posthumously awarded the William & Mary Alumni Association's Alumni Medal.
*   The Laurel B. Clark and David M. Brown Aerospace Medicine Academic Center, located at the Naval Aerospace Medical Institute, is named after him.
*   The Captain David Brown Aerospace and Medical Research Endowment was established in his memory to help deserving students attending Eastern Virginia Medical School.
*   The planetarium of [Arlington Public Schools](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arlington_Public_Schools "Arlington Public Schools"), from which Brown graduated, was renamed the [David M. Brown Planetarium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arlington_Public_Schools#Special_facilities "Arlington Public Schools").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_M._Brown#cite_note-:0-2)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_M._Brown#cite_note-9)
*   The Dave Brown Memorial Park in [Friendswood, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friendswood,_Texas "Friendswood, Texas"), is named after him.
*   The annual Astronaut Dave Brown Memorial gymnastics meet is held at the [College of William & Mary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_of_William_&_Mary "College of William & Mary") in his honor, where Dave Brown was a gymnast.
*   Yorktown High School Crew Team Men's Varsity 8 boat name Captain David M. Brown - c. 2003
*   Circle Oil Hill Elementary of [Circle USD 375](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circle_USD_375 "Circle USD 375") in Kansas grants a scholarship each year - David Brown Hopes & Dreams Scholarship. This scholarship was first awarded in 2005.

**David McDowell Brown** (April 16, 1956 – February 1, 2003) was a [United States Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Navy "United States Navy")[captain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain_(United_States_O-6) "Captain (United States O-6)") and [NASA astronaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_astronaut "NASA astronaut"). He died on his first [spaceflight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spaceflight "Spaceflight"), when the [Space Shuttle _Columbia_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia") ([STS-107](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-107 "STS-107")) disintegrated during orbital reentry into the Earth's atmosphere. Brown became an astronaut in 1996 but had not served on a space mission prior to the [_Columbia_ disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia disaster"). He was posthumously awarded the [Congressional Space Medal of Honor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congressional_Space_Medal_of_Honor "Congressional Space Medal of Honor").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_M._Brown#cite_note-1)

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=David_M._Brown&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Brown was born on April 16, 1956, in [Arlington, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arlington,_Virginia "Arlington, Virginia"). As a youth, he attended McKinley Elementary School and Swanson Middle School, and graduated from [Yorktown High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yorktown_High_School_(Virginia) "Yorktown High School (Virginia)") in Arlington in 1974. Brown was a member of the [Boy Scouts of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boy_Scouts_of_America "Boy Scouts of America") and achieved its second-highest rank, [Life Scout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_Scout "Life Scout"). [[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_M._Brown#cite_note-:0-2) He received a [Bachelor of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Science "Bachelor of Science") degree in [biology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biology "Biology") from the [College of William & Mary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_of_William_&_Mary "College of William & Mary") in 1978, and a [Doctor of Medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_of_Medicine "Doctor of Medicine") from the [Eastern Virginia Medical School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Virginia_Medical_School "Eastern Virginia Medical School") in 1982.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_M._Brown#cite_note-:0-2)

## Military career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=David_M._Brown&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Military career")]

Brown joined the [U.S. Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Navy "U.S. Navy") after his internship at the [Medical University of South Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_University_of_South_Carolina "Medical University of South Carolina"). Upon completion of [flight surgeon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flight_surgeon "Flight surgeon") training in 1984, Brown reported to the Navy Branch Hospital in [Adak, Alaska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adak,_Alaska "Adak, Alaska"), as Director of Medical Services.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_M._Brown#cite_note-3) He was then assigned to [Carrier Air Wing Fifteen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carrier_Air_Wing_Fifteen "Carrier Air Wing Fifteen") which deployed aboard the [aircraft carrier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aircraft_carrier "Aircraft carrier")[USS _Carl Vinson_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Carl_Vinson "USS Carl Vinson") in the Western Pacific. In 1988, Brown became the only flight surgeon in a 10-year period to be chosen for pilot training. He was ultimately designated a [Naval Aviator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naval_Aviator "Naval Aviator") in 1990 at [NAS Chase Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAS_Chase_Field "NAS Chase Field") in [Beeville, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beeville,_Texas "Beeville, Texas"), ranking number one in his class. Brown was then sent for training and carrier qualification in the [A-6E Intruder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A-6_Intruder "A-6 Intruder"). In 1991, he reported to the Naval Strike Warfare Center at [NAS Fallon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAS_Fallon "NAS Fallon"), [Nevada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nevada "Nevada"), serving as a Strike Leader Attack Training Syllabus Instructor and a Contingency Cell Planning Officer. Brown was also qualified in the [F/A-18 Hornet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F/A-18_Hornet "F/A-18 Hornet") and deployed from Japan in 1992 aboard [USS _Independence_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Independence_(CV-62) "USS Independence (CV-62)") flying the A-6E with [VA-115](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VFA-115 "VFA-115"). In 1995, he reported to the [U.S. Naval Test Pilot School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Naval_Test_Pilot_School "U.S. Naval Test Pilot School") at [NAS Patuxent River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAS_Patuxent_River "NAS Patuxent River"), Maryland as their flight surgeon, where Brown also flew the [T-38 Talon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T-38_Talon "T-38 Talon").

Brown logged over 2,700 flight hours, with 1,700 in high-performance military aircraft. He was qualified as the first pilot in NASA T-38 aircraft and held a [Federal Communications Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Communications_Commission "Federal Communications Commission") (FCC) issued Technician Class [amateur radio license](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amateur_radio_license "Amateur radio license") with the [call sign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Call_sign "Call sign") KC5ZTC.

Brown also served as President of the International Association of Military Flight Surgeon Pilots, an associate fellow at the [Aerospace Medical Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerospace_Medical_Association "Aerospace Medical Association"), and a member of the Society of U.S. Naval Flight Surgeons.

## NASA career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=David_M._Brown&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: NASA career")]

Selected by [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA") in April 1996, Brown reported to the [Johnson Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_Space_Center "Johnson Space Center") in August 1996. He completed two years of training and evaluation and was qualified for flight assignment as a mission specialist. Brown was initially assigned to support payload development for the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station"), followed by the astronaut support team responsible for orbiter cockpit setup, crew strap-in, and landing recovery.

On April 21, 2001, Brown appeared on [ESPN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESPN "ESPN") as an expert on [g-force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G-force "G-force") loading on the human body that led to the cancellation of the [Firestone Firehawk 600](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Firestone_Firehawk_600 "Firestone Firehawk 600")[CART](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Championship_Auto_Racing_Teams "Championship Auto Racing Teams") race.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_M._Brown#cite_note-4)

Brown flew aboard [Space Shuttle _Columbia_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia") on [STS-107](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-107 "STS-107"), logging 15 days, 22 hours, and 20 minutes in space from January 16 to February 1, 2003. The flight was a dedicated science and research mission. Working 24 hours a day, in two alternating shifts, the crew successfully conducted approximately 80 experiments. On February 1, 2003, all seven members of _Columbia'_ s crew perished during reentry, 16 minutes before the scheduled landing.

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=David_M._Brown&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Personal life")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fe/US_Navy_030312-N-2147L-001_U.S._Navy_Capt._David_M._Brown%2C_NASA_Astronaut_laid_to_rest.jpg/250px-US_Navy_030312-N-2147L-001_U.S._Navy_Capt._David_M._Brown%2C_NASA_Astronaut_laid_to_rest.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:US_Navy_030312-N-2147L-001_U.S._Navy_Capt._David_M._Brown,_NASA_Astronaut_laid_to_rest.jpg)

Brown's funeral services at [Arlington National Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arlington_National_Cemetery "Arlington National Cemetery") on March 12, 2003

The only unmarried member of the STS-107 crew, Brown had previously been romantically involved with NASA engineer Ann Micklos. The couple ended their relationship shortly before the mission and remained close friends until his death.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_M._Brown#cite_note-5) The crew of STS-107 had formed a close friendship during their training, and Brown had been preparing a video to commemorate this once they returned from the mission. He is buried in [Arlington National Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arlington_National_Cemetery "Arlington National Cemetery").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_M._Brown#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_M._Brown#cite_note-7)

## Tributes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=David_M._Brown&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Tributes")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0f/David_M._Brown_Planetarium%2C_Arlington%2C_Virginia_.jpg/250px-David_M._Brown_Planetarium%2C_Arlington%2C_Virginia_.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:David_M._Brown_Planetarium,_Arlington,_Virginia_.jpg)

The David M. Brown Planetarium in Arlington County, Virginia

*   Asteroid [51825 Davidbrown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/51825_Davidbrown "51825 Davidbrown") was named in honor of Brown.
*   Lunar crater D. Brown is named after Brown.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_M._Brown#cite_note-8)
*   Brown Hall, in the Columbia Village apartments, at the [Florida Institute of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida_Institute_of_Technology "Florida Institute of Technology") is named after him.
*   He is the first person to be posthumously awarded the William & Mary Alumni Association's Alumni Medal.
*   The Laurel B. Clark and David M. Brown Aerospace Medicine Academic Center, located at the Naval Aerospace Medical Institute, is named after him.
*   The Captain David Brown Aerospace and Medical Research Endowment was established in his memory to help deserving students attending Eastern Virginia Medical School.
*   The planetarium of [Arlington Public Schools](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arlington_Public_Schools "Arlington Public Schools"), from which Brown graduated, was renamed the [David M. Brown Planetarium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arlington_Public_Schools#Special_facilities "Arlington Public Schools").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_M._Brown#cite_note-:0-2)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_M._Brown#cite_note-9)
*   The Dave Brown Memorial Park in [Friendswood, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friendswood,_Texas "Friendswood, Texas"), is named after him.
*   The annual Astronaut Dave Brown Memorial gymnastics meet is held at the [College of William & Mary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_of_William_&_Mary "College of William & Mary") in his honor, where Dave Brown was a gymnast.
*   Yorktown High School Crew Team Men's Varsity 8 boat name Captain David M. Brown - c. 2003
*   Circle Oil Hill Elementary of [Circle USD 375](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circle_USD_375 "Circle USD 375") in Kansas grants a scholarship each year - David Brown Hopes & Dreams Scholarship. This scholarship was first awarded in 2005.

**Laurel Blair Clark** (née **Salton**; March 10, 1961 – February 1, 2003) was an American [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA") astronaut, medical doctor, [United States Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Navy "United States Navy")[captain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain_(U.S._Navy) "Captain (U.S. Navy)"), and [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") mission specialist. She died along with her six fellow crew members in the [Space Shuttle _Columbia_ disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia disaster"). Clark was posthumously awarded the [Congressional Space Medal of Honor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congressional_Space_Medal_of_Honor "Congressional Space Medal of Honor").

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laurel_Clark&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Clark was born in [Ames, Iowa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ames,_Iowa "Ames, Iowa"), but considered [Racine, Wisconsin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racine,_Wisconsin "Racine, Wisconsin"), her hometown. She graduated from [William Horlick High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Horlick_High_School "William Horlick High School") in [Racine, Wisconsin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racine,_Wisconsin "Racine, Wisconsin") in 1979. She enrolled at the [University of Wisconsin–Madison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Wisconsin%E2%80%93Madison "University of Wisconsin–Madison"), where she received a [Bachelor of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Science "Bachelor of Science") degree in [zoology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zoology "Zoology") in 1983, and a [Doctor of Medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_of_Medicine "Doctor of Medicine") in 1987. Clark was also a member of the [Gamma Phi Beta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamma_Phi_Beta "Gamma Phi Beta") sorority at the university. She held a [Federal Communications Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Communications_Commission "Federal Communications Commission") (FCC) issued Technician Class [amateur radio license](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amateur_radio_license "Amateur radio license") with the [call sign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Call_sign "Call sign") KC5ZSU.

## Military career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laurel_Clark&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Military career")]

During medical school, Clark did active duty training with the Diving Medicine Department at the [United States Navy Experimental Diving Unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Navy_Experimental_Diving_Unit "United States Navy Experimental Diving Unit") in March 1987. After completing medical school, she underwent postgraduate medical education in pediatrics from 1987 to 1988 at the [National Naval Medical Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Naval_Medical_Center "National Naval Medical Center"). The following year, Clark completed Navy undersea medical officer training at the Naval Undersea Medical Institute in [Groton, Connecticut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groton,_Connecticut "Groton, Connecticut"), and diving medical officer training at the Naval Diving and Salvage Training Center in [Panama City, Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panama_City,_Florida "Panama City, Florida"). She was designated a Radiation Health Officer and Undersea Medical Officer. Clark was then assigned as the [Submarine Squadron 14](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Submarine_Squadron_14 "Submarine Squadron 14") Medical Department Head in [Holy Loch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Loch "Holy Loch"), Scotland. During that assignment, she dove with Navy divers and [Naval Special Warfare Unit Two SEALs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Navy_SEALs "United States Navy SEALs") and performed many medical evacuations from US submarines. After two years of operational experience, Clark was designated as a Naval Submarine Medical Officer and Diving Medical Officer.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-NASAbio-1)

Clark underwent six months of aeromedical training at the Naval Aerospace Medical Institute at [NAS Pensacola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAS_Pensacola "NAS Pensacola") in [Pensacola, Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pensacola,_Florida "Pensacola, Florida"), and was designated as a Naval Flight Surgeon. She was stationed at [MCAS Yuma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MCAS_Yuma "MCAS Yuma"), [Arizona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arizona "Arizona"), and assigned as Flight Surgeon Marine Attack Squadron 211 (VMA-211), a Marine Corps [AV-8B Harrier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AV-8B_Harrier "AV-8B Harrier") squadron. Clark made several deployments, including one overseas to the Western Pacific, practiced medicine in austere environments, and flew on multiple aircraft. Her squadron won the Marine Attack Squadron of the Year award for its successful deployment. Clark was then assigned as the Group Flight Surgeon for [Marine Aircraft Group 13](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_Aircraft_Group_13 "Marine Aircraft Group 13") (MAG-13).

Before her selection as an astronaut candidate, Clark served as a Flight Surgeon for Training Squadron 86 ([VT-86](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VT-86 "VT-86")), the [Naval Flight Officer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naval_Flight_Officer "Naval Flight Officer") advanced training squadron for tactical jets at NAS Pensacola. She was Board Certified by the National Board of Medical Examiners and held a Wisconsin Medical License, and her military qualifications included Radiation Health Officer, Undersea Medical Officer, Diving Medical Officer, Submarine Medical Officer, and Naval Flight Surgeon. Clark was also a Basic Life Support Instructor, Advanced Cardiac Life Support Provider, Advanced Trauma Life Support Provider, and Hyperbaric Chamber Advisor. Clark was a member of the [Aerospace Medical Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerospace_Medical_Association "Aerospace Medical Association") and the Society of U.S. Naval Flight Surgeons.

## NASA career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laurel_Clark&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: NASA career")]

Selected by NASA in April 1996, Clark reported to the [Johnson Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_Space_Center "Johnson Space Center") in [Houston, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston,_Texas "Houston, Texas"), in August 1996.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-2) After completing two years of training and evaluation, she was qualified for flight assignment as a mission specialist. From July 1997 to August 2000, Clark worked in the Astronaut Office Payloads/Habitability Branch. She flew aboard [STS-107](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-107 "STS-107"), logging 15 days, 22 hours and 21 minutes in space.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-NASAbio-1)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-3)

### Space flight experience

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laurel_Clark&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Space flight experience")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b4/LaurelClarkSTS107.jpg/250px-LaurelClarkSTS107.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:LaurelClarkSTS107.jpg)

Laurel Clark during STS-107

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2f/STS-107_Laurel_Clark.jpg/250px-STS-107_Laurel_Clark.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STS-107_Laurel_Clark.jpg)

Laurel Clark looks through an overhead window on the aft flight deck of the Shuttle.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-4)

Main article: [STS-107](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-107 "STS-107")

STS-107 _Columbia_ – The 16-day flight was a dedicated science and research mission. Working 24 hours a day, in two alternating shifts, the crew successfully conducted approximately 80 experiments. Clark's bioscience experiments included gardening in space, as she discussed only days before her death in an interview with [Milwaukee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milwaukee "Milwaukee") media near her Wisconsin hometown. The STS-107 mission ended abruptly on February 1, 2003, when _Columbia_ disintegrated and her crew perished during re-entry, 16 minutes before scheduled landing.

Clark also recorded inside the cockpit during _Columbia_'s descent into the Earth's atmosphere on a small digital camera.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-5)

Clark's final message to her friends and family was through an email sent from _Columbia_.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-7) In the released text of the email, Clark called the planet magnificent, and explained that while she spends much of the time working back in Spacehab and away from the sights of Earth, "whenever I do get to look out, it is glorious." Clark found that taking photos of the Earth was challenging, "Keeping my fingers crossed that they're in sharp focus." Clark also shared some of the intriguing effects of micro gravity on human physiology, such as constant challenge to stay adequately hydrated due to an "almost non-existent" sense of thirst.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-8)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laurel_Clark&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Clark is survived by her husband, fellow former U.S. Navy captain and NASA flight surgeon Dr. Jonathan Clark (who was part of an official NASA panel that prepared the final 400-page report about the _Columbia_ disaster), and son Iain who was born in 1996.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-10) She was also a member of the Olympia Brown Unitarian Universalist Church in Racine, Wisconsin.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-11)

## Tributes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laurel_Clark&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Tributes")]

*   [Asteroid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asteroid "Asteroid")[51827 Laurelclark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/51827_Laurelclark "51827 Laurelclark") was named for Clark.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-12)
*   Clark Hill in the [Columbia Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Hills_(Mars) "Columbia Hills (Mars)") on [Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars "Mars") was named for Clark.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-13)
*   L. Clark, an interior crater of the lunar crater [Apollo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_(crater) "Apollo (crater)"), was named for Clark.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-15)
*   Clark Hall, in the Columbia Village Suites at the [Florida Institute of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida_Institute_of_Technology "Florida Institute of Technology"), is named after her.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] The apartments were initially planned to be named the Crane Creek Suites, but were renamed in 2008 to commemorate the _Columbia_ crew.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]
*   The Laurel Salton Clark Memorial Fountain in Racine, Wisconsin is named for her.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-16)
*   In 2004, the Naval Aerospace Medicine Institute named its Aerospace Medicine Academic Center in [Pensacola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pensacola "Pensacola") after Clark and David M. Brown[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-17)
*   Clark Auditorium at Walter Reed National Military Medical Center, Bethesda, Maryland is named for her and displays uniforms, training manuals, and personal items that belonged to her.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-18)
*   The Scottish band [Runrig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Runrig "Runrig") pays tribute to Clark on the 2016 album _[The Story](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Story\_(Runrig\_album) "The Story (Runrig album)")_. The final track, "Somewhere", ends with a recording of her voice.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-19) Clark was a Runrig fan and had a wake up call with Runrig's "Running to the Light". She took their 2001 _[The Stamping Ground](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Stamping\_Ground "The Stamping Ground")_ CD into space with her. When the shuttle disintegrated the CD was found among the debris that reached the Earth's surface, and was presented to the band by her family.
*   [Northrop Grumman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northrop_Grumman "Northrop Grumman") named a [Cygnus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cygnus_(spacecraft) "Cygnus (spacecraft)") cargo spacecraft [S.S. _Laurel Clark_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cygnus_NG-19 "Cygnus NG-19").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-20)

**Laurel Blair Clark** (née **Salton**; March 10, 1961 – February 1, 2003) was an American [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA") astronaut, medical doctor, [United States Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Navy "United States Navy")[captain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain_(U.S._Navy) "Captain (U.S. Navy)"), and [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") mission specialist. She died along with her six fellow crew members in the [Space Shuttle _Columbia_ disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia disaster"). Clark was posthumously awarded the [Congressional Space Medal of Honor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congressional_Space_Medal_of_Honor "Congressional Space Medal of Honor").

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laurel_Clark&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Clark was born in [Ames, Iowa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ames,_Iowa "Ames, Iowa"), but considered [Racine, Wisconsin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racine,_Wisconsin "Racine, Wisconsin"), her hometown. She graduated from [William Horlick High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Horlick_High_School "William Horlick High School") in [Racine, Wisconsin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racine,_Wisconsin "Racine, Wisconsin") in 1979. She enrolled at the [University of Wisconsin–Madison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Wisconsin%E2%80%93Madison "University of Wisconsin–Madison"), where she received a [Bachelor of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Science "Bachelor of Science") degree in [zoology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zoology "Zoology") in 1983, and a [Doctor of Medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_of_Medicine "Doctor of Medicine") in 1987. Clark was also a member of the [Gamma Phi Beta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamma_Phi_Beta "Gamma Phi Beta") sorority at the university. She held a [Federal Communications Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Communications_Commission "Federal Communications Commission") (FCC) issued Technician Class [amateur radio license](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amateur_radio_license "Amateur radio license") with the [call sign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Call_sign "Call sign") KC5ZSU.

## Military career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laurel_Clark&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Military career")]

During medical school, Clark did active duty training with the Diving Medicine Department at the [United States Navy Experimental Diving Unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Navy_Experimental_Diving_Unit "United States Navy Experimental Diving Unit") in March 1987. After completing medical school, she underwent postgraduate medical education in pediatrics from 1987 to 1988 at the [National Naval Medical Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Naval_Medical_Center "National Naval Medical Center"). The following year, Clark completed Navy undersea medical officer training at the Naval Undersea Medical Institute in [Groton, Connecticut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groton,_Connecticut "Groton, Connecticut"), and diving medical officer training at the Naval Diving and Salvage Training Center in [Panama City, Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panama_City,_Florida "Panama City, Florida"). She was designated a Radiation Health Officer and Undersea Medical Officer. Clark was then assigned as the [Submarine Squadron 14](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Submarine_Squadron_14 "Submarine Squadron 14") Medical Department Head in [Holy Loch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Loch "Holy Loch"), Scotland. During that assignment, she dove with Navy divers and [Naval Special Warfare Unit Two SEALs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Navy_SEALs "United States Navy SEALs") and performed many medical evacuations from US submarines. After two years of operational experience, Clark was designated as a Naval Submarine Medical Officer and Diving Medical Officer.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-NASAbio-1)

Clark underwent six months of aeromedical training at the Naval Aerospace Medical Institute at [NAS Pensacola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAS_Pensacola "NAS Pensacola") in [Pensacola, Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pensacola,_Florida "Pensacola, Florida"), and was designated as a Naval Flight Surgeon. She was stationed at [MCAS Yuma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MCAS_Yuma "MCAS Yuma"), [Arizona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arizona "Arizona"), and assigned as Flight Surgeon Marine Attack Squadron 211 (VMA-211), a Marine Corps [AV-8B Harrier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AV-8B_Harrier "AV-8B Harrier") squadron. Clark made several deployments, including one overseas to the Western Pacific, practiced medicine in austere environments, and flew on multiple aircraft. Her squadron won the Marine Attack Squadron of the Year award for its successful deployment. Clark was then assigned as the Group Flight Surgeon for [Marine Aircraft Group 13](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_Aircraft_Group_13 "Marine Aircraft Group 13") (MAG-13).

Before her selection as an astronaut candidate, Clark served as a Flight Surgeon for Training Squadron 86 ([VT-86](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VT-86 "VT-86")), the [Naval Flight Officer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naval_Flight_Officer "Naval Flight Officer") advanced training squadron for tactical jets at NAS Pensacola. She was Board Certified by the National Board of Medical Examiners and held a Wisconsin Medical License, and her military qualifications included Radiation Health Officer, Undersea Medical Officer, Diving Medical Officer, Submarine Medical Officer, and Naval Flight Surgeon. Clark was also a Basic Life Support Instructor, Advanced Cardiac Life Support Provider, Advanced Trauma Life Support Provider, and Hyperbaric Chamber Advisor. Clark was a member of the [Aerospace Medical Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerospace_Medical_Association "Aerospace Medical Association") and the Society of U.S. Naval Flight Surgeons.

## NASA career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laurel_Clark&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: NASA career")]

Selected by NASA in April 1996, Clark reported to the [Johnson Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_Space_Center "Johnson Space Center") in [Houston, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston,_Texas "Houston, Texas"), in August 1996.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-2) After completing two years of training and evaluation, she was qualified for flight assignment as a mission specialist. From July 1997 to August 2000, Clark worked in the Astronaut Office Payloads/Habitability Branch. She flew aboard [STS-107](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-107 "STS-107"), logging 15 days, 22 hours and 21 minutes in space.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-NASAbio-1)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-3)

### Space flight experience

Laurel Clark looks through an overhead window on the aft flight deck of the Shuttle.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-4)

Main article: [STS-107](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-107 "STS-107")

STS-107 _Columbia_ – The 16-day flight was a dedicated science and research mission. Working 24 hours a day, in two alternating shifts, the crew successfully conducted approximately 80 experiments. Clark's bioscience experiments included gardening in space, as she discussed only days before her death in an interview with [Milwaukee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milwaukee "Milwaukee") media near her Wisconsin hometown. The STS-107 mission ended abruptly on February 1, 2003, when _Columbia_ disintegrated and her crew perished during re-entry, 16 minutes before scheduled landing.

Clark also recorded inside the cockpit during _Columbia_'s descent into the Earth's atmosphere on a small digital camera.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-5)

Clark's final message to her friends and family was through an email sent from _Columbia_.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-7) In the released text of the email, Clark called the planet magnificent, and explained that while she spends much of the time working back in Spacehab and away from the sights of Earth, "whenever I do get to look out, it is glorious." Clark found that taking photos of the Earth was challenging, "Keeping my fingers crossed that they're in sharp focus." Clark also shared some of the intriguing effects of micro gravity on human physiology, such as constant challenge to stay adequately hydrated due to an "almost non-existent" sense of thirst.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-8)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laurel_Clark&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Clark is survived by her husband, fellow former U.S. Navy captain and NASA flight surgeon Dr. Jonathan Clark (who was part of an official NASA panel that prepared the final 400-page report about the _Columbia_ disaster), and son Iain who was born in 1996.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-10) She was also a member of the Olympia Brown Unitarian Universalist Church in Racine, Wisconsin.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-11)

## Tributes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laurel_Clark&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Tributes")]

*   [Asteroid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asteroid "Asteroid")[51827 Laurelclark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/51827_Laurelclark "51827 Laurelclark") was named for Clark.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-12)
*   Clark Hill in the [Columbia Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Hills_(Mars) "Columbia Hills (Mars)") on [Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars "Mars") was named for Clark.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-13)
*   L. Clark, an interior crater of the lunar crater [Apollo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_(crater) "Apollo (crater)"), was named for Clark.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-15)
*   Clark Hall, in the Columbia Village Suites at the [Florida Institute of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida_Institute_of_Technology "Florida Institute of Technology"), is named after her.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] The apartments were initially planned to be named the Crane Creek Suites, but were renamed in 2008 to commemorate the _Columbia_ crew.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]
*   The Laurel Salton Clark Memorial Fountain in Racine, Wisconsin is named for her.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-16)
*   In 2004, the Naval Aerospace Medicine Institute named its Aerospace Medicine Academic Center in [Pensacola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pensacola "Pensacola") after Clark and David M. Brown[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-17)
*   Clark Auditorium at Walter Reed National Military Medical Center, Bethesda, Maryland is named for her and displays uniforms, training manuals, and personal items that belonged to her.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-18)
*   The Scottish band [Runrig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Runrig "Runrig") pays tribute to Clark on the 2016 album _[The Story](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Story\_(Runrig\_album) "The Story (Runrig album)")_. The final track, "Somewhere", ends with a recording of her voice.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-19) Clark was a Runrig fan and had a wake up call with Runrig's "Running to the Light". She took their 2001 _[The Stamping Ground](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Stamping\_Ground "The Stamping Ground")_ CD into space with her. When the shuttle disintegrated the CD was found among the debris that reached the Earth's surface, and was presented to the band by her family.
*   [Northrop Grumman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northrop_Grumman "Northrop Grumman") named a [Cygnus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cygnus_(spacecraft) "Cygnus (spacecraft)") cargo spacecraft [S.S. _Laurel Clark_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cygnus_NG-19 "Cygnus NG-19").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-20)

Biographical Data

Lyndon B. Johnson Space Center
Houston, Texas  77058  National Aeronautics and

KALPANA CHAWLA (PH.D.)
NASA ASTRONAUT (DECEASED)

PERSONAL DATA:  Born in Karnal, India.  Died on February 1, 2003 over the southern
United States when Space Shuttle Columbia  and her crew perished during entry, 16
minutes prior to scheduled landing.  She is survived by her husband.  Kalpana Chawla
enjoyed flying, hiking, back-  packing, and reading.  She held a  Certificated Flight
Instructor's license with airplane and glider ratings, Commercial Pilot's licenses for single-
and multi-engine land and seaplanes, and Gliders, and instrument rating for airplanes.  She
enjoyed flying aerobatics and tail-  wheel airplanes.

EDUCATION:  Graduated from Tagore School, Karnal, India, in 1976.  Bachelor of
science degree in aeronautical engineering from Punjab Engineering College, India, 1982.
Master of science degree in aerospace engineering from University of Texas, 1984.
Doctorate of philosophy in aerospace engineering from University of Colorado, 1988.

AWARDS:  Posthumously awarded the Congressional Space Medal of Honor, the NASA
Space Flight Medal, and the NASA Distinguished Service Medal.

EXPERIENCE:  In 1988, Kalpana Chawla started work at NASA Ames Research Center in the area of powered  -lift computational
fluid dynamics.  Her research concentrated on simulation of complex air flows encountered around aircraft such as the Harrier  in
" ground-effect."  Following completion of this project she supported research in mapping of flow solvers to parallel computers, and
testing of these solvers by carrying out powered lift computations.  In 1993 Kalpana Chawla joined Overset Methods Inc., Los
Altos, California, as Vice President and Research Scientist to form a team with other researchers specializing in simulation of
moving multiple body problems.  She was responsible for development and implementation of efficient techniques to perform
aerodynamic optimization.  Results of various projects that Kalpana Chawla participated in are documented in technical conference
papers and journals.

NASA EXPERIENCE:  Selected by NASA in December 1994, Kalpana Chawla reported to the Johnson Space Center in March
1995 as an astronaut candidate in the 15th Group of Astronauts.  After completing a year of training and evaluation, she was
assigned as crew representative to work technical issues for the Astronaut Office EVA/Robotics and Computer Branches.  Her
assignments included work on development of Robotic Situational Awareness Displays and testing space shuttle control software in
the Shuttle Avionics Integration Laboratory.  In November, 1996, Kalpana Chawla was assigned as mission specialist and prime
robotic arm operator on ST S  -87.  In January 1998, she was assigned as crew representative for shuttle and station flight crew
equipment, and subsequently served as lead for Astronaut Office’s Crew Systems and Habitability section.  She flew on STS-87
(1997) and STS-107 (2003), logging 30 days, 14 hours and 54 minutes in space.

SPACE FLIGHT EXPERIENCE:  ST S-  87  Columbia  (November 19 to December 5, 1997).  STS-87 was the fourth U.S
Microgravity P ayload flight and focused on experiments designed to study how the weightless environment of space affects various
physical processes, and on observations of the Sun's outer atmospheric layers.  Two members of the crew performed an EVA
(spacewalk) which featured the manual capture of a Spartan satellite, in addition to testing EVA tools and procedures for future
Space Station assembly.  ST S-87 made 252 orbits of the Earth, traveling  6.5 million miles in in 376 hours and 34 minutes.

ST S-  107  Columbia  (January 16 to February 1, 2003).  T he 16  -day flight was a dedicated science and research mission.  Working
24 hours a day, in two alternating shifts, the crew successfully conducted approximately 80 experiments.  The STS-107 mission
ended abruptly on February 1, 2003 when Space Shuttle Columbia  and  the  crew perished during entry, 16 minutes prior to
scheduled landing.

Biographical Data

Lyndon B. Johnson Space Center
Houston, Texas  77058  National Aeronautics and

KALPANA CHAWLA (PH.D.)
NASA ASTRONAUT (DECEASED)

PERSONAL DATA:  Born in Karnal, India.  Died on February 1, 2003 over the southern
United States when Space Shuttle Columbia  and her crew perished during entry, 16
minutes prior to scheduled landing.  She is survived by her husband.  Kalpana Chawla
enjoyed flying, hiking, back-  packing, and reading.  She held a  Certificated Flight
Instructor's license with airplane and glider ratings, Commercial Pilot's licenses for single-
and multi-engine land and seaplanes, and Gliders, and instrument rating for airplanes.  She
enjoyed flying aerobatics and tail-  wheel airplanes.

EDUCATION:  Graduated from Tagore School, Karnal, India, in 1976.  Bachelor of
science degree in aeronautical engineering from Punjab Engineering College, India, 1982.
Master of science degree in aerospace engineering from University of Texas, 1984.
Doctorate of philosophy in aerospace engineering from University of Colorado, 1988.

AWARDS:  Posthumously awarded the Congressional Space Medal of Honor, the NASA
Space Flight Medal, and the NASA Distinguished Service Medal.

EXPERIENCE:  In 1988, Kalpana Chawla started work at NASA Ames Research Center in the area of powered  -lift computational
fluid dynamics.  Her research concentrated on simulation of complex air flows encountered around aircraft such as the Harrier  in
" ground-effect."  Following completion of this project she supported research in mapping of flow solvers to parallel computers, and
testing of these solvers by carrying out powered lift computations.  In 1993 Kalpana Chawla joined Overset Methods Inc., Los
Altos, California, as Vice President and Research Scientist to form a team with other researchers specializing in simulation of
moving multiple body problems.  She was responsible for development and implementation of efficient techniques to perform
aerodynamic optimization.  Results of various projects that Kalpana Chawla participated in are documented in technical conference
papers and journals.

NASA EXPERIENCE:  Selected by NASA in December 1994, Kalpana Chawla reported to the Johnson Space Center in March
1995 as an astronaut candidate in the 15th Group of Astronauts.  After completing a year of training and evaluation, she was
assigned as crew representative to work technical issues for the Astronaut Office EVA/Robotics and Computer Branches.  Her
assignments included work on development of Robotic Situational Awareness Displays and testing space shuttle control software in
the Shuttle Avionics Integration Laboratory.  In November, 1996, Kalpana Chawla was assigned as mission specialist and prime
robotic arm operator on ST S  -87.  In January 1998, she was assigned as crew representative for shuttle and station flight crew
equipment, and subsequently served as lead for Astronaut Office’s Crew Systems and Habitability section.  She flew on STS-87
(1997) and STS-107 (2003), logging 30 days, 14 hours and 54 minutes in space.

SPACE FLIGHT EXPERIENCE:  ST S-  87  Columbia  (November 19 to December 5, 1997).  STS-87 was the fourth U.S
Microgravity P ayload flight and focused on experiments designed to study how the weightless environment of space affects various
physical processes, and on observations of the Sun's outer atmospheric layers.  Two members of the crew performed an EVA
(spacewalk) which featured the manual capture of a Spartan satellite, in addition to testing EVA tools and procedures for future
Space Station assembly.  ST S-87 made 252 orbits of the Earth, traveling  6.5 million miles in in 376 hours and 34 minutes.

ST S-  107  Columbia  (January 16 to February 1, 2003).  T he 16  -day flight was a dedicated science and research mission.  Working
24 hours a day, in two alternating shifts, the crew successfully conducted approximately 80 experiments.  The STS-107 mission
ended abruptly on February 1, 2003 when Space Shuttle Columbia  and  the  crew perished during entry, 16 minutes prior to
scheduled landing.

Biographical Data

Lyndon B. Johnson Space Center
Houston, Texas  77058  National Aeronautics and
Space Administration

KALPANA CHAWLA (PH.D.)
NASA ASTRONAUT (DECEASED)

PERSONAL DATA:  Born in Karnal, India.  Died on February 1, 2003 over the southern
United States when Space Shuttle Columbia  and her crew perished during entry, 16
minutes prior to scheduled landing.  She is survived by her husband.  Kalpana Chawla
enjoyed flying, hiking, back-  packing, and reading.  She held a  Certificated Flight
Instructor's license with airplane and glider ratings, Commercial Pilot's licenses for single-
and multi-engine land and seaplanes, and Gliders, and instrument rating for airplanes.  She
enjoyed flying aerobatics and tail-  wheel airplanes.

EDUCATION:  Graduated from Tagore School, Karnal, India, in 1976.  Bachelor of
science degree in aeronautical engineering from Punjab Engineering College, India, 1982.
Master of science degree in aerospace engineering from University of Texas, 1984.
Doctorate of philosophy in aerospace engineering from University of Colorado, 1988.

AWARDS:  Posthumously awarded the Congressional Space Medal of Honor, the NASA
Space Flight Medal, and the NASA Distinguished Service Medal.

EXPERIENCE:  In 1988, Kalpana Chawla started work at NASA Ames Research Center in the area of powered  -lift computational
fluid dynamics.  Her research concentrated on simulation of complex air flows encountered around aircraft such as the Harrier  in
" ground-effect."  Following completion of this project she supported research in mapping of flow solvers to parallel computers, and
testing of these solvers by carrying out powered lift computations.  In 1993 Kalpana Chawla joined Overset Methods Inc., Los
Altos, California, as Vice President and Research Scientist to form a team with other researchers specializing in simulation of
moving multiple body problems.  She was responsible for development and implementation of efficient techniques to perform
aerodynamic optimization.  Results of various projects that Kalpana Chawla participated in are documented in technical conference
papers and journals.

NASA EXPERIENCE:  Selected by NASA in December 1994, Kalpana Chawla reported to the Johnson Space Center in March
1995 as an astronaut candidate in the 15th Group of Astronauts.  After completing a year of training and evaluation, she was
assigned as crew representative to work technical issues for the Astronaut Office EVA/Robotics and Computer Branches.  Her
assignments included work on development of Robotic Situational Awareness Displays and testing space shuttle control software in
the Shuttle Avionics Integration Laboratory.  In November, 1996, Kalpana Chawla was assigned as mission specialist and prime
robotic arm operator on ST S  -87.  In January 1998, she was assigned as crew representative for shuttle and station flight crew
equipment, and subsequently served as lead for Astronaut Office’s Crew Systems and Habitability section.  She flew on STS-87
(1997) and STS-107 (2003), logging 30 days, 14 hours and 54 minutes in space.

SPACE FLIGHT EXPERIENCE:  ST S-  87  Columbia  (November 19 to December 5, 1997).  STS-87 was the fourth U.S
Microgravity P ayload flight and focused on experiments designed to study how the weightless environment of space affects various
physical processes, and on observations of the Sun's outer atmospheric layers.  Two members of the crew performed an EVA
(spacewalk) which featured the manual capture of a Spartan satellite, in addition to testing EVA tools and procedures for future
Space Station assembly.  ST S-87 made 252 orbits of the Earth, traveling  6.5 million miles in in 376 hours and 34 minutes.

ST S-  107  Columbia  (January 16 to February 1, 2003).  T he 16  -day flight was a dedicated science and research mission.  Working
24 hours a day, in two alternating shifts, the crew successfully conducted approximately 80 experiments.  The STS-107 mission
ended abruptly on February 1, 2003 when Space Shuttle Columbia  and  the  crew perished during entry, 16 minutes prior to
scheduled landing.

RICK DOUGLAS HUSBAND  (COLONEL, USAF)
NASA ASTRONAUT (DECEASED)
PERSONAL DATA:  Born Ju  ly 12, 1957, in Amarillo, Texas.  Died on February
1, 2003 over the southern United States when Space Shuttle Columbia  and her
crew perished during entry, 16 minutes prior to scheduled landing.  He is survived
by his wife and their two children.  He enjoyed singing, water and snow skiing,
cycling, and spending time with his family.
EDUCATION:  Graduated from Amarillo High School, Amarillo, Texas, in
1975.  Received a bachelor of science degree in mechanical engineering from
Texas Tech University in 1980, and a master of science degree in mechanical
engineering from California State University, Fresno, in 1990.

ORGANIZATIONS:  Member of the Society of Experimental Test Pilots, Tau
Beta Pi, Air Force Association, and the T exas T ech Ex-Students Association.

AWARDS:  Posthumously awarded the Congressional Space Medal of Honor, the
NASA Space Flight Medal, the NASA Distinguished Service Medal, and the Defense Distinguished Service Medal
(DDSM.

SPECIAL HONORS:  Distinguished Graduate of AFROTC, Undergraduate Pilot Training, Squadron Officers School, F  -4
Instructor School, and USAF Test Pilot School; Outstanding Engineering Student Award, Texas Tech University, 1980; F-4
T actical Air Command Instructor Pilot of the Year (1987); named a 1997 Distinguished Engineer of the College of Engineering,
Texas Tech University.  Military decorations include the Meritorious Service Medal with two Oak Leaf Clusters, the Aerial
Achievement Medal, the Air Force Commendation Medal, the National Defense Service Medal, two NASA Group Achievement
Awards for work on the X-38 Development T eam and the Orbiter Upgrade Definition T eam.

EXPERIENCE:  After graduation from Texas Tech University in May 1980, Husband was commissioned a second lieutenant in
the USAF and attended pilot training at Vance Air Force Base (AFB), Oklahoma.  He graduated in October 1981, and was
assigned to F-4 training at Homestead AFB, Florida.  After completion of F-4 training in September 1982, Husband was assigned
to Moody AFB, Georgia flying the F-4E.  From September  to November 1985, he attended F-4 Instructor School at Homestead
AFB and was assigned as an F-4E instructor pilot and academic instructor at George AFB, California in December 1985.  In
December 1987, Husband was assigned to Edwards AFB, California, where  he attended the USAF Test Pilot School.  Upon
completion of Test Pilot School, Husband served as a test pilot flying the F-4 and all five models of the F-15.  In the F-15
Combined Test Force, Husband was the program manager for the Pratt & Whitney F100-PW-229 increased performance engine,
and also served as the F-15 Aerial Demonstration Pilot.  In June 1992, Husband was assigned to the Aircraft and Armament
Evaluation Establishment at Boscombe Down, England, as an exchange test pilot with the Royal Air Force.  At Boscombe Down,
Husband was the Tornado GR1 and GR4 Project Pilot and served as a test pilot in the Hawk, Hunter, Buccaneer, Jet Provost,
Tucano, and Harvard.  He logged over 3800 hours of flight time in more than 40 different types of aircraft.

NASA EXPERIENCE:  Husband was selected as an astronaut candidate by NASA in December 1994.  He reported to the
Johnson Space Center in March 1995 to begin a year of training and evaluation.  Upon completion of training, he was named the
Astronaut Office representative for Advanced Projects at Johnson Space Center, working on Space Shuttle Upgrades, the Crew
Return Vehicle (CRV) and studies to return to the Moon and travel to Mars.  He also served as Chief of Safety for the Astronaut
Office.  Husband was pilot on ST S  -96 (1999) and crew commander on STS-107 (2003), logging 24 days, 51 hours and 33 minutes
in space.
SPACE FLIGHT EXPERIENCE:  ST S-  96 Discovery (May 27 to June 6, 1999) was a 10-  day mission during which the crew
performed the first docking with the International Space Station and delivered 4 tons of logistics and supplies in preparation for
the arrival of the first crew to live on the station early next year.  The mission was accomplished in 153 Earth orbits, traveling
4 million miles in 9 days, 19 hours and 13 minutes.

fluid dynamics.  Her research concentrated on simulation of complex air flows encountered around aircraft such as the Harrier  in

Altos, California, as Vice President and Research Scientist to form a team with other researchers specializing in simulation of
moving multiple body problems.  She was responsible for development and implementation of efficient techniques to perform
aerodynamic optimization.  Results of various projects that Kalpana Chawla participated in are documented in technical conference
papers and journals.

1995 as an astronaut candidate in the 15th Group of Astronauts.  After completing a year of training and evaluation, she was

the Shuttle Avionics Integration Laboratory.  In November, 1996, Kalpana Chawla was assigned as mission specialist and prime

(1997) and STS-107 (2003), logging 30 days, 14 hours and 54 minutes in space.
